# The Candle as a Way into Natural Philosophy

The speaker opens his course with a plain statement of purpose. Over these lectures he intends to present the chemical history of a candle. He offers the lectures in return for the honour the audience does him by coming to see the proceedings, treating the exchange as a courtesy owed rather than a performance given.

## Why Return to the Candle

This is not new ground for him. He has lectured on this subject on a former occasion, and he admits that if he were left to his own will he would repeat it almost every year. His reason is that the subject of the candle holds abundant interest. It is not a narrow topic. The candle opens onto many different departments of philosophy, and the reach of the subject is wider still: every law governing any part of the universe comes into play in the phenomena of a candle.

From this he draws a methodological conclusion. Studying the physical phenomena of a candle is the best and most open way into the study of natural philosophy. A beginner needs no specialised apparatus to start, only attention to something burning in front of him. The speaker therefore does not apologise for an old topic. In his judgment no newer topic would be better than the candle, and probably none would be as good.

## Tone and Audience

He sets out the terms on which he will proceed. He intends to treat the subject honestly, seriously, and philosophically. He also declares his chosen audience: he means to address the young people rather than the adults in the room. He claims the privilege of speaking to young people as a young person himself, and he notes that he has addressed young audiences in this way on former occasions. He is aware that his words will be published to the world, but that knowledge will not stop him from speaking familiarly to the young listeners in front of him.

## Natural Candles: Candle-Wood

Before turning to manufactured candles, the speaker remarks that some candles are great curiosities, and that some kinds of trees are particularly famous for burning well. His chief example is a substance called candle-wood, taken from some bogs in Ireland.

Candle-wood is a hard, strong, excellent wood, well suited to resisting force, and it also burns well. Where it is found, people make splinters and torches from it. It burns like a candle and gives a very good light. For these reasons the speaker regards it as one of the best illustrations of the general nature of a candle.

Its value as an illustration comes from the functions it performs. Candle-wood provides fuel. It provides a means of bringing that fuel to the place of chemical action. It provides a regular and gradual supply of air to the same place. And it produces heat and light. Because it combines all of these functions in one material, candle-wood is in effect a natural candle, and it serves as a reference model for the manufactured candles that follow.

## Dips

The first manufactured type is the candle commonly called a dip. Dips are made by hanging lengths of cotton by a loop and dipping them in melted tallow. Each length is then cooled and re-dipped, over and over, until tallow builds up around the cotton.

## Miners' Candles

Very small candles were used by miners in coal mines. In former times miners had to supply their own candles. It was believed that a small candle would ignite fire-damp in the mines less readily than a large one, so miners used small candles partly for safety and partly for economy. These candles were made at 20, 30, 40, or 60 to the pound. In time they were replaced by the steel-mill, and the steel-mill was later replaced by the Davy lamp and other safety lamps.

## A Candle from the Royal George

The speaker's next specimen concerns durability. Colonel Pasley reportedly took a candle from the wreck of the Royal George. It had been sunk in the sea and exposed to salt water for many years. The example demonstrates that candles can be preserved well over long periods. Although this candle is cracked and broken, it burns regularly when lit, and its tallow returns to its natural condition once melted.

## Materials and the Stearin Process

The speaker credits Mr. Field of Lambeth with supplying him with many illustrations of candles and their materials. He then turns to those materials.

The first is suet, which is the fat of the ox. The speaker believes Russian tallow is used to make dips. A significant advance came when Gay-Lussac, or someone who shared the knowledge with him, converted tallow into stearin. The practical difference is visible in use. Modern candles are clean rather than greasy like ordinary tallow candles. The drips from a modern candle can be scraped off and powdered without soiling anything.

The conversion proceeds in stages:

1. **Saponification.** Tallow is first boiled with quicklime to make a soap.
2. **Acid decomposition.** The soap is then decomposed with sulphuric acid, which removes the lime. This decomposition leaves the fat rearranged as stearic acid.
3. **By-product.** Glycerin is produced at the same time as the stearic acid. Glycerin is a sugar, or a substance similar to sugar, and it comes out of the tallow during this chemical change.
4. **Pressing.** The oil is then pressed out of the stearic acid. As the pressure increases, the oily part carries the impurities out with it.
5. **Casting.** The substance left after pressing is melted and cast into candles.

The products of this process are stearin candles, made from stearin derived from tallow.

## Other Candle Materials

The speaker closes this survey with the remaining materials. Sperm candles come from the purified oil of the spermaceti whale. Candles are also made from yellow beeswax and from refined beeswax. Paraffin is a curious substance from which candles are made, and it can be obtained from the bogs of Ireland. Finally, a kind of wax brought from Japan is a new material for making candles; it became available only after Japan was forced open to outside access.

# The Candle as a Way into Natural Philosophy

The speaker begins his course with a plain statement of his purpose, which is to set before his hearers, over these lectures, the chemical history of a candle. His audience honours him by coming to see the proceedings, and he offers the lectures in return. He regards them as a courtesy he owes to those who have come, and he does not present them as a performance.

## Why Return to the Candle

He has lectured on this subject on a former occasion, and he admits that if he were left to his own will he would repeat it almost every year. The subject of the candle holds abundant interest, and it is far from narrow. It opens onto many different departments of philosophy, and its reach goes wider still, for every law that governs any part of the universe comes into play in the phenomena of a candle.

From this the speaker draws a conclusion about method. The study of the physical phenomena of a candle is, he holds, the best and the most open door by which to enter the study of natural philosophy. The beginner needs no special apparatus to start. He needs only to attend to the thing that burns before him. The candle is therefore an old topic, and the speaker makes no apology for it; in his judgment no newer topic would serve better, and probably none would serve as well.

## Tone and Audience

He next lays down the terms on which he means to proceed, and he promises to treat the subject honestly, seriously and philosophically. He has also chosen his hearers, and they are the young people in the room, not the adults. He claims the privilege of speaking to the young as one who is young himself, and he has addressed young audiences in this manner on former occasions. He knows well that his words will be published to the world; but that knowledge will not prevent him from speaking familiarly to the young listeners who sit in front of him.

## Natural Candles: Candle-Wood

Before he comes to the candles that men manufacture, the speaker observes that some candles are great curiosities, and that certain kinds of trees are especially famous for burning well. His chief example is a substance called candle-wood, which is taken out of some of the bogs of Ireland.

Candle-wood is hard and strong, an excellent wood, well able to resist force; and it burns well besides. Where it is found, people split it into splinters and make torches of it. It burns like a candle and gives a very good light. On account of these properties the speaker counts it among the best illustrations of the general nature of a candle.

Candle-wood owes its value as an illustration to the work it does. It supplies fuel. It supplies a means of carrying that fuel to the place where the chemical action goes on. It supplies a regular and gradual stream of air to that same place, and it yields heat and light. Since one material performs every one of these offices, candle-wood is in effect a natural candle, and the manufactured candles which follow may all be measured against it.

## Dips

The first manufactured kind is the candle commonly called a dip. To make dips, lengths of cotton are hung up by a loop and plunged into melted tallow. Each length is then cooled and dipped again, and this is repeated many times over, until a coat of tallow has built up around the cotton.

## Miners' Candles

Miners used very small candles in the coal mines. In former times the miner had to find his own candles, and it was believed that a small candle would fire the fire-damp less readily than a large one; hence the miner chose small candles, partly for safety and partly for economy. These candles were made at 20, 30, 40 or 60 to the pound. The steel-mill in due course took their place, and the steel-mill in its turn gave way to the Davy lamp and to other safety lamps.

## A Candle from the Royal George

The speaker's next specimen bears upon durability. Colonel Pasley, it is said, took a candle from the wreck of the Royal George, where it had lain sunk in the sea and exposed to salt water for many years. The specimen shows that a candle may keep well over a long period. This candle is cracked and broken, yet when it is lit it burns regularly, and its tallow, once melted, returns to its natural condition.

## Materials and the Stearin Process

The speaker acknowledges Mr. Field of Lambeth, who furnished him with many illustrations of candles and of the materials from which they are made. To those materials he then turns.

The first is suet, which is the fat of the ox. Russian tallow, the speaker believes, is the stuff of which dips are made. A considerable advance came when Gay-Lussac, or some one who shared the knowledge with him, converted tallow into stearin. Use makes the difference between the two plain to every eye. Ordinary tallow candles are greasy, whereas the modern candle is clean, and the drippings from it may be scraped off and powdered without soiling anything.

The conversion proceeds by stages:

1. **Saponification.** Tallow is first boiled with quicklime, and a soap is formed.
2. **Acid decomposition.** The soap is next decomposed with sulphuric acid, which takes away the lime; and the fat is left rearranged as stearic acid.
3. **By-product.** Glycerin is produced at the same time as the stearic acid. Glycerin is a sugar, or a substance very like sugar, and it comes out of the tallow in the course of this chemical change.
4. **Pressing.** The oil is then pressed out of the stearic acid, and as the pressure is increased the oily part carries the impurities away with it.
5. **Casting.** What remains after the pressing is melted and cast into candles.

The products of this process are stearin candles, and the stearin of which they are made is derived from tallow.

## Other Candle Materials

The speaker completes his survey with the remaining materials. Sperm candles are made from the purified oil of the spermaceti whale. Candles are also made from yellow beeswax and from refined beeswax. Paraffin, a curious substance which may be obtained from the bogs of Ireland, serves for candles as well. Last of all there is a kind of wax brought from Japan, a new material for the candle-maker, which reached us only after Japan had been forced open to outside access.
